item.title: Climate variability and human adaptation in late quaternary Northeast Asia: A critical review of paleoenvironmental and archaeological records from Northeast China and Primorye of Russia
item.dc:creator: Xinrong Zhang, Jing Xu, Alexandra Romanova, Yuri Mikishin, Yuri Vostretsov, Peter Jia, … (+1)
item.description:
Anthropocene — matched: paleoclimate, last glacial maximum, interglacial, Holocene, Quaternary, radiocarbon
Northeast China and Russian Primorye lie at the confluence of the East Asian summer monsoon, Siberian High, and Pacific maritime circulation. The region experienced pronounced glacial-interglacial variability and served as a corridor for human dispersal among Siberia, East Asia, and the Americas. This review synthesises palaeoecological and archaeological evidence, principally from the past ca. 50 ka. Environmental records trace a transition from the cold, arid steppe of the Last Glacial Maximum (ca. 26.5–19.0 ka BP) to warmer, more forested Holocene landscapes, while revealing strong spatial heterogeneity and abrupt events. Although the ≥146 ka Harbin cranium predates the main review interval, it establishes a Middle Pleistocene hominin presence; securely dated archaeological sequences considered here begin in the Late Pleistocene. These records document developments from Upper Palaeolithic lithic industries to Neolithic sedentism, millet agriculture, and Bronze Age sociopolitical complexity. A central limitation is the spatial separation of most palaeoclimatic archives and archaeological sites. Their differing chronological resolution further restricts direct causal attribution, leaving many proposed climate-culture relationships as working hypotheses. We therefore advocate co-located multiproxy transects, improved chronological control, and tephrochronological correlation. A site-by-site appraisal of radiocarbon, OSL, and U-series chronologies identifies relationships that are currently testable. The Boisman-Krounovka sequence suggests that resource breadth and specialisation may mediate vulnerability to environmental change, although the roles of social organisation, mobility, and demography remain unresolved. Northeast Asia thus offers a framework for generating and testing hypotheses about climatic variability, demographic processes, and cultural change rather than demonstrating simple climate-driven causation.

item.title: The internal variability modulates marine heatwave duration changes by day-to-day ocean memory in the recent decades
item.dc:creator: Di Sun, Lu Dong, Fengfei Song, Zhao Jing, Shijie Zeng, Lixin Wu
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea surface temperature, CMIP, ensemble, heat wave
Abstract The duration of marine heatwaves (MHWs) determines the cumulative thermal stress imposed on marine organisms, thereby strongly influencing the severity of ecological consequences. Recently, day-to-day ocean memory, quantified by a first-order sea surface temperature (SST) autocorrelation model, has been found as an effective metric to depict the duration of MHWs, due to its consistent climatological distribution and trends with MHW duration in the observations. However, the relative importance of external forcing and internal variability in modulating the day-to-day ocean memory and, more importantly, its relationship with MHW duration, remain unclear. In this study, we employ 100 ensemble members of CESM2 and 32 CMIP6 models to analyze the roles of external forcing and internal variability in the day-to-day ocean memory and MHW duration. We find that internal variability dominates the trends of day-to-day ocean memory in the recent decades and further modulates the trends of MHW duration, particularly in the tropical oceans. The zonal gradient of SST trends over the tropical Pacific emerges as a key feature of the internal variability. By combining a stochastic climate model framework with a mixed-layer heat budget, we further reveal that ocean mixing and dynamics are the primary processes through which internal variability modulates trends in day-to-day ocean memory, whereas SST-surface heat flux feedback provides a secondary contribution and variations in mixed-layer depth play negligible roles. This study demonstrates that internal variability exerts a considerable influence on MHW duration through its modulation on day-to-day ocean memory, providing crucial evidence and a new perspective for understanding and predicting MHW duration in a warming climate.

item.title: Regional climatic change following the Eocene–Oligocene Transition in central northern Tibet
item.dc:creator: Leyi Li, Hong Chang, Philippe Sorrel, Jing Lei, Balázs Bradák, Xiaoke Qiang, … (+1)
item.description:
Geological Society of America Bulletin — matched: paleoclimate, proxy, sea level
The Eocene–Oligocene Transition (EOT) constitutes one of the most dramatic climatic changes in the Cenozoic era; it is characterized by global cooling, increasing aridity, extinction of fauna and flora, and a major drop of global sea level. However, how continental settings responded to global climatic change after the EOT event has still received little consideration. Here we report a high-resolution and well-dated terrestrial EOT record from the Tuotuohe Basin (central northern Tibetan Plateau). Sedimentary facies, fossil evidence, new proxy, and climate modeling data suggest a transition from warm and dry to cool and wet climatic conditions ca. 33 Ma, in contrast with other records from the Tibetan Plateau that commonly document drier conditions after the EOT (ca. 34 Ma). Having considered the potential forcing mechanisms, we propose that the Indian monsoon likely expanded into the Tuotuohe Basin after the EOT due to a combination of factors, such as the land-sea pressure gradient caused by the retreat of the Paratethys Sea, tectonic uplift in central northern Tibet and increased cross-equatorial pressure gradients. This study opens new perspectives for paleoclimate model simulations around the EOT that encompasses major environmental reorganizations at the continent scale, such as the Mongolian Re-modeling (faunal turnovers of Paleogene mammals from the Mongolian Plateau) and the Grande Coupure (extinction of a large number of European native mammals).

item.title: Ice breakup dynamics on the Kuskokwim River: climatic trends and hydro-meteorological drivers
item.dc:creator: Sergio Gómez Muñoz, K. E. Lindenschmidt, J. S. Ostman, Crane Johnson
item.description:
Hydrological Sciences Journal — matched: Arctic, reanalysis, extreme event
River ice breakup is a critical hydrological process governing flood risk and transportation in sub-arctic regions. This study investigates hydroclimatic drivers of breakup timing on the lower Kuskokwim River, Alaska, synthesizing a 102-year observational record (1924–2025) with ERA5 reanalysis. Statistical analysis reveals a winter warming trend driving a phenological advancement of 0.77 days per decade, yet inter-decadal timing variance remains persistently high. Classifying historical events into early, normal, and late categories demonstrate that despite varying spring warming rates, the ice cover consistently requires ∼ 231°C-days of thermal accumulation to reach structural susceptibility. Late breakups are delayed by deep spring snowpacks acting as thermal insulators, not by differing thermal requirements. While atmospheric heat pre-conditions the ice, pre-breakup discharge acts as an independent mechanical trigger. These results provide a categorical framework for tracking warming trajectories and contextualizing extreme events in data-limited basins.

item.title: Monsoon zonal seesaw: Development of the South Asian monsoon aridified North Africa in the Cenozoic
item.dc:creator: Zihan Yin, Ji Nie, William R. Boos, Alex Farnsworth, Zhongshi Zhang, Yonggang Liu, … (+3)
item.description:
Science Advances — matched: paleoclimate, ensemble
North Africa experienced a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic. Meanwhile, the South Asian monsoon underwent substantial intensification, largely driven by the uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau. Here, we demonstrate that the two events, which greatly shaped the paleoenvironment and modern regional climate, are not independent responses to paleogeography changes; rather, the former is primarily driven by the latter through the monsoon-desert mechanism, in which South Asian monsoon diabatic heating produces large-scale subsidence and aridity over North Africa. Using multiple ensembles of paleoclimate simulations and a model for the atmospheric response to imposed diabatic heating, we show that the intensification and poleward shift of Asian monsoon rainfall each make comparable contributions to the aridification of North Africa. Our findings identify a persistent dynamical pathway linking the South Asian and North African monsoons and suggest that it played a major role in early Cenozoic North African aridification, while its climatic expression at other times depended on the relative strengths of competing forcings.
